newsitem.title: HONG KONG: U.S. mayor untroubled by Asian campaign gifts.
newsitem.headline: U.S. mayor untroubled by Asian campaign gifts.

text.p: San Francisco Mayor Willie Brown said on Monday voters in his city were not troubled by the kind of political campaign gifts from Asian donors that have landed fellow Democrats Bill Clinton and Al Gore in hot water.

The U.S. Democratic Party has returned millions of dollars of contributions to the 1996 campaign of President Clinton and running mate Al Gore over charges that China and Asian business executives made donations to sway U.S. policy.
Brown, touring Asia to drum up business for San Francisco, said the city has 52,000 Chinese voters who contribute significantly to the municipal tax base.
"There is not a politician who is not eager to get Asian contributions and Asian votes," Brown told reporters after a speech to the American Chamber of Commerce in Hong Kong.

The San Francisco trade delegation was the latest in a string of visits by American politicians and business executives who see opportunities in China's growing economic power and want to take advantage of a recent thaw in political tensions.

Brown said the group had already snagged some business from China for the city during earlier stops in Beijing and Shanghai and hopes to draw even more from Asia based on the city's strengths in financial services, the multi-media industry and proximity to Silicon Valley's high-tech companies.
Brown said China may locate a trade office in San Francisco.
After Hong Kong, Brown and the delegation will travel to Taipei, Taiwan.

Brown, who was the first black and the longest-serving speaker of the California state assembly before being elected mayor in 1995, said he supports Clinton's stance of continuing most-favoured-nation (MFN) trade status for China -- a goal that may be politically more difficult to achieve this year.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin warned on Sunday the campaign contributions controversy and China's human rights record along with the mounting Sino-U.S. trade deficit would make winning congressional approval for MFN renewal more difficult.
Brown, who met China's President Jiang Zemin and Vice-Premier Zhu Rongji, said he believed they want "to establish a bridge between U.S. senior elected officials and Chinese officials.

"In the years ahead they believe there will be two major powers -- the PRC and the USA. They believe they may be superior as relates to the economy and they are very proud themselves," Brown told reporters.

On Hong Kong as a business centre after the July 1 handover from Britain to China, Brown said the Chinese officials told him: "They said candidly it serves our interest to have Hong Kong continue as it is currently, and we intend to see that that happens."
